caption:
The Nasdaq fell 2.6% on Thursday, its steepest one-day drop since early June, as fears about AI spending hit tech stocks.
Chipmakers led the slide, and Meta fell 7% after its first cash outflow in more than a decade.

Is the AI spending boom starting to crack?

paragraphs.text: The Nasdaq Composite fell 694 points, or 2.6 percent, to 26,008.86 on Thursday, October 22, 2026, as concerns about the cost of the artificial intelligence buildout weighed on technology shares, Reuters reported. It was the index's steepest one-day decline since early June. The S&P 500 lost 1.2 percent to 7,663.43, while the Dow Jones Industrial Average ended nearly unchanged, up 0.02 percent at 52,867.98.

Invezz reported that the session was the S&P 500's worst since July. Trading volume was heavier than usual, with 18.79 billion shares changing hands compared with an average of 17.19 billion over the previous 20 sessions, according to Reuters.

Semiconductor stocks took the largest losses. The Philadelphia SE Semiconductor Index fell 6.7 percent, its biggest daily percentage drop since June 23, leaving it more than 26 percent below its June 22 record close, although it remains up more than 50 percent for the year, Reuters reported. Intel, AMD, Sandisk and Marvell each fell more than 8 percent.

Invezz reported that Micron Technology fell 6 percent and Nvidia fell 4 percent. CoreWeave, which rents out AI computing capacity, dropped more than 10 percent on continuing concerns about its debt and financing costs.

Meta Platforms fell about 7 percent even though its quarterly results beat analyst expectations. The company reported its first cash outflow in more than a decade, which Reuters tied to AI spending, and announced plans for a two-for-one stock split that uses non-voting shares to raise money for its AI expansion.
Tesla also declined despite reporting unexpectedly positive free cash flow and cutting its 2026 capital spending plans, according to both outlets.

Paul Nolte, senior wealth adviser and market strategist at Murphy & Sylvest, told Reuters that investors were starting to see holes in the AI story and that technology was the only part of the market under real pressure. In an earlier version of the Reuters report, Oliver Pursche of Wealthspire Advisors described a hypersensitivity around earnings for AI-related stocks and said the return on that investment was still unknown.

Oil prices added to the pressure. Crude reached a five-month high after Iran-backed Houthi forces struck targets in Saudi Arabia, raising concern that conflict in the Middle East could keep inflation elevated. Brent settled at $113.03 a barrel, according to Invezz. Reuters reported that markets were pricing in a possible 25 basis point interest rate increase by the end of the year.

Several companies outside the AI trade rose. Spotify gained 11.1 percent after forecasting fourth-quarter profit above estimates, Blackstone rose 8.4 percent, Lockheed Martin climbed 7 percent after raising its forecasts and Procter and Gamble added 5.6 percent, Reuters reported. Of the 111 S&P 500 companies that had reported third-quarter results, 83 percent beat analyst expectations, according to LSEG data cited by both outlets.

The selloff did not come from weak results. Meta and Tesla both reported numbers that topped forecasts, yet their shares fell, which suggests investors are now judging AI companies on how much cash the buildout consumes rather than on quarterly earnings alone. Chipmakers, whose revenue depends on that spending continuing, absorbed the sharpest losses.

The next test comes as more large technology companies report quarterly results and update their capital spending plans, which will show whether the AI buildout keeps its pace after the market's reaction on October 22.
